strengths: Clear problem identification: Section 2.3 provides a useful, quantified analysis showing that foundation FM priors (via both plug-in D-Flow and interleaving FlowDPS) currently lag behind domain-specific and even untrained priors (DIP) for inverse problems; Table 1 and Fig. 2 support this across difficulty levels.

The warm-start strategy is well-motivated: the concentration-of-measure argument (Sec. 3.1) that D-Flow's initialization (Eq. 2.4) lands off the training shell of the flow is a genuinely insightful explanation for why existing prior-strengthening fails, and the learnable-time shortcut (Eq. 3.5) is a natural remedy that is also efficient (NFE=3).

The sharp Gaussianity regularization is sensibly designed: the observation that D-Flow's chi-square negative log-likelihood is nearly flat near its minimum (Fig. 3) justifies the shell constraint with closed-form projection (Eq. 3.9), and the extension to the few-shot setting via simplex-constrained linear combinations (Eq. 3.10) is a reasonable adaptation for scientific IPs.

Broad and largely fair empirical evaluation: 3 datasets, 4 linear tasks, 6 metrics, comparisons against plug-in, interleaving, prompt-enabled, domain-specific, and untrained prior baselines; ablation (Table 6) dissects the contribution of each component, and the few-shot experiments on InverseBench (LIS, MRI) demonstrate gains outside standard image restoration.

Consistent improvements over the main plug-in competitor D-Flow across most settings, and results approaching domain-specific prior performance (Table 4), supporting the central claim that foundation FM priors can be made practical for IPs.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: both components are simple modifications of D-Flow — a learnable starting time on the flow and a norm-shell constraint/projection. The authors themselves acknowledge that spherical Gaussian constraints exist (Yang et al., 2024) and that D-Flow already uses warm-start initialization; the contribution is primarily an empirical fix, and the sharpness claim rests on a heuristic rather than any new theory.

Dependence on strong assumptions that limit scope: the simple-distortion setting explicitly assumes x and y are close (Sec. 3.1), and the few-shot setting assumes instance images close to x are available; the method's behavior when these assumptions fail (e.g., nonlinear or heavily degraded forward models) is not characterized.

Unresolved surjectivity concern: the plug-in formulation's validity hinges on Gθ being (approximately) surjective, which is acknowledged as theoretically unsupported and checked only by one small image-regression experiment (Table 2); this leaves the method's foundation somewhat empirical.

Inconsistencies in the headline claims: the paper states FMPlug is 'the overall winner by all metrics but CLIPIQA and MUSIQ,' yet in several settings (e.g., AFHQ super-resolution and Gaussian blur in Tables 3, 7, 8) FMPlug's CLIPIQA/MUSIQ scores are dramatically worse than competitors (e.g., 0.20 vs 0.65 CLIPIQA), and DIP often ties or beats FMPlug-W on no-reference metrics; perceptual-quality tradeoffs deserve a more careful treatment than the current framing.

Potential fairness issues in comparisons: NFE budgets differ substantially (FMPlug 3, D-Flow 6, FlowDPS/FlowChef 28), and while lower NFE favors FMPlug, the optimization setups (optimizer, learning rates, calibration) differ in ways that are hard to attribute; no error bars or significance tests are reported over the 100-image evaluations despite PSNR differences sometimes being small (e.g., vs DIP on inpainting).

Some design elements are ad hoc and under-validated: the mean-variance calibration (Eq. 3.6) has minor effect at the tested noise level (Table 13) and its motivation/heuristics are not analyzed; hyperparameter sensitivity (e.g., learning rates 0.5 for z, 0.005 for t; epsilon = 0.025) is not studied, and no code release is stated, weakening reproducibility.

Few-shot results, while improving over DIP and D-Flow, remain clearly behind the domain-specific-prior reference (Red-diff: 36.55 vs 31.83 PSNR on LIS), so the 'closing the gap' narrative holds mainly for simple-distortion image restoration rather than the scientific setting emphasized.

strengths: The paper identifies and carefully documents a real and practically relevant problem: foundation flow-matching priors underperform domain-specific and even untrained priors on inverse problems, supported by controlled comparisons (Table 1, Fig. 2) that isolate the prior while fixing the solver.

The proposed method is simple and efficient: the time-dependent warm-start (learnable t in Eq. 3.5) plus a hard shell projection achieves strong gains over D-Flow across three datasets and four tasks (e.g., Gaussian deblur PSNR 26.26 vs 23.64 on DIV2K), with very low NFE (3), and the ablation in Table 6 shows both components contribute.

The evaluation breadth is above average for this area: image restoration tasks plus two scientific IPs from InverseBench, multiple metrics, prompt-enabled variants of competitors, and a few-shot extension for narrow-domain imaging.

The writing is generally clear, the CoM-based motivation for why D-Flow's initialization lands off the training shell is an interesting intuition, and hyperparameters for all baselines are reported in the appendix.
weaknesses: The theoretical motivation is heuristic and partially inconsistent with the method. The concentration-of-measure argument is used to justify constraining ||z||2, but after warm-starting the effective input alpha_t*y + beta_t*z is itself not Gaussian and generally off the training shell, so the same critique the authors level at D-Flow's initialization applies to their own formulation. Only the norm is constrained; the argument says nothing about direction, and no evidence is given that the learned solutions actually lie near the manifold the model was trained on.

Novelty over D-Flow (Ben-Hamu et al., 2024) is modest: the method is essentially D-Flow with (a) a learnable start time on the flow and (b) a hard norm constraint replacing the soft chi-squared penalty (the authors themselves note spherical Gaussian constraints exist in Yang et al., 2024). The substantial gains of even FMPlug-Plain over D-Flow in Table 6 (25.16 vs 23.64 PSNR) suggest part of the improvement comes from unexamined implementation differences (optimizer, NFE, calibration) rather than the two proposed components, which is not fully ablated.

The central setting is narrow and arguably close to assuming the answer. The simple-distortion setting requires x and y to be close so that y can be injected into the flow; no experiments probe robustness when this assumption degrades (beyond kernel-size variation in a motivation figure), no nonlinear forward operators are tested, and the few-shot extension assumes the target lies near a convex combination of provided instances.

Evidence for several claims is thin. The surjectivity 'test' (Table 2) is a training-set image regression on 1000 images with no held-out evaluation, far from establishing that G_theta can represent arbitrary reasonable x. The claim that prior strengthening techniques are 'almost useless' (Sec. 2.3.2) rests on a quick empirical check reported only in passing. The headline claim of closing the gap to domain-specific priors is only partially supported: Table 4 shows FMPlug (FD) still trails domain-specific methods on several metrics (e.g., MUSIQ 28.77 vs 64.63 for OT-ODE), and it consistently loses to competitors on CLIPIQA/MUSIQ in Tables 7-12, hinting at perceptual-quality issues not discussed.
Statistical rigor is missing: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests across the 100-image evaluations, despite differences between some methods being small.

No code release is mentioned, the generalization of the calibration procedure across backbone models is untested (everything uses SD3-Medium), and the paper lacks a limitations discussion, despite significant scope restrictions (linear operators, closeness assumptions, image objects only).

strengths: The paper identifies and carefully documents a real and underexplored problem: foundation FM priors underperform domain-specific and even untrained priors for inverse problems (Table 1, Fig. 2, Section 2.3), and prior 'strengthening' heuristics are shown to be nearly ineffective. This problem framing is valuable and clearly argued.

The proposed method is motivated by a concrete theoretical observation: the concentration-of-measure argument (Theorem 3.1) explains why D-Flow's initialization (Eq. 2.4) and its χ²-based Gaussianity regularizer are misaligned with how FM models are actually trained (thin-shell support). The resulting time-dependent warm-start (Eq. 3.5) and shell constraint (Eq. 3.7-3.9) are simple, well-motivated, and cheap (closed-form projection, NFE = 3).

The empirical evaluation is broad: 3 datasets (AFHQ, DIV2K, RealSR) × 4 linear tasks, 6+ metrics, multiple SOTA baselines (D-Flow, FlowDPS, FlowChef, with and without text prompts), a domain-specific-prior comparison (Table 4), two scientific IPs from InverseBench, and an ablation study (Table 6) that cleanly separates the contributions of warm-start and regularization.

The warm-start strategy substantially improves upon the direct competitor D-Flow across nearly all distortion-level metrics, and FMPlug (FD) approaches domain-specific SOTA performance on some tasks (e.g., Gaussian blur PSNR in Table 4), which is genuine progress toward the paper's stated goal.

Implementation details, optimizer settings, NFE, and task configurations are provided in the appendix, supporting reproducibility; the few-shot extension (Section 3.3) extends applicability beyond image restoration.
weaknesses: The core warm-start idea leans heavily on the assumption that x and y are close (simple-distortion setting), effectively using the measurement itself as a proxy for the ground truth during initialization. This borders on information leakage for restoration tasks and limits the method's scope; the few-shot variant partially addresses this, but there the method still trails the domain-specific Red-Diff by large margins (31.83 vs 36.55 PSNR on LIS; 23.26 vs 28.71 on MRI), so the central claim of 'closing the gap' is only partially supported.

FMPlug consistently underperforms on perceptual/no-reference metrics (CLIPIQA and MUSIQ): e.g., CLIPIQA of 0.18-0.27 vs FlowChef's ~0.6 on super-resolution across datasets (Table 3), and MUSIQ of ~28-30 vs OT-ODE's ~64 (Table 4). The paper acknowledges FMPlug wins on 'all metrics but CLIPIQA and MUSIQ,' but this pattern is consistent with over-fitting to the data-fitting term and could indicate blurry or over-smooth outputs—only a small qualitative figure set is offered to rebut this.

The theoretical justification is informal. The claim that Gθ's behavior off the training shell 'can be wild' is asserted, not established; surjectivity of Gθ is verified only by a single image-regression test on 1000 DIV2K images (Table 2). The mean-variance calibration (Eq. 3.6) is a heuristic patch whose benefit is marginal at σ = 0.03 and only appears at σ = 0.06.

The technical novelty is modest: a learnable initialization time plus a norm/shell constraint with projection. Individual ingredients (spherical Gaussian constraints, warm-starting) exist in prior work (the paper itself cites Yang et al., 2024); the contribution is mainly in the combination and the diagnosis of why existing variants fail.

Sensitivity analysis is thin: the impact of ε (fixed at 0.025), learning rates, and the learnable t initialization across tasks is not systematically studied. No error bars or significance testing are reported despite using 100 images per dataset, making some metric differences (e.g., FMPlug vs FMPlug-W of ~0.2 dB PSNR) hard to interpret.

FMPlug applied with a domain-specific prior (FMPlug (DS) in Table 4) underperforms DS baselines on several metrics (e.g., Gaussian blur CLIPIQA 0.24 vs PnP-Flow 0.66, DIST 0.77 vs 0.20), raising questions about whether the method genuinely strengthens priors or merely exploits the measurement proximity; no code release is mentioned, which further limits reproducibility.

strengths: The paper identifies and clearly documents an interesting and practically relevant phenomenon: foundation flow-matching priors substantially underperform domain-specific FM priors and even untrained priors (DIP) as plug-in priors for inverse problems (Tab. 1, Fig. 3, Tab. 16), and prior 'strengthening' ideas (D-Flow's Gaussian likelihood regularizer, FlowDPS's text prompts) provide little benefit (Sec. 2.3.2).

The proposed methods are simple, well-motivated, and grounded in concentration-of-measure intuition: the time-dependent warm-start (Eq. 3.5) exploits the closeness of x and y to shortcut the flow, and the sharp shell constraint (Eq. 3.7/3.9) fixes the flatness problem of D-Flow's chi-square regularizer (Fig. 4). The closed-form projection keeps implementation clean (Alg. 1/2).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 3 datasets, 4 linear tasks at 512x512, scientific IPs from InverseBench (LIS, MRI, BKH), ablations of both components (Tab. 5), learned warm-start time behavior consistent with theory (Tab. 6), sensitivity to epsilon and NFE (Tabs. 7-8), variance across random initializations (Tab. 17), and few-shot instance count (Tab. 18).

Honest treatment of failure modes and limitations: the MRI gap is attributed to few-shot guidance violating the assumption, supported by correlation analysis between learned weights and instance-to-target distance (Spearman -0.71); the caveat about no-reference metrics is discussed; the few-shot assumption and its violation scenarios are explicitly stated (Sec. 3.3, 4.2).
Computational profile is favorable among plug-in methods (Tab. 9): fewer NFEs than interleaving methods and lower memory than D-Flow, with the best PSNR/LPIPS in most settings.
weaknesses: The central assumption—that a ground-truth-like instance (y, A^†y, E(y), or a few-shot instance close to x) is available for warm-start—substantially narrows the scope of the method. For simple distortions this makes FMPlug close to a strong post-processing/refinement of the measurement rather than a pure generative prior; the gains over DIP and D-Flow partly stem from this extra guidance, which the baselines (D-Flow random init, FlowDPS/FlowChef) do not equally exploit in all settings. The paper should more carefully separate gains attributable to the prior vs. the injected instance.

The theoretical support is heuristic. The shell-concentration argument for why D-Flow's initialization fails (Sec. 3.1) is intuitive but informal—no result is proven that G_theta behaves badly off the training shell, or that the warm-start + shell constraint provably improves reconstruction. The 'surjectivity' claim rests on a single empirical regression test on DIV2K (Tab. 2).

The method is essentially a combination of two simple components (learnable start-time and norm constraint); novelty is moderate, and the advantage over domain-specific priors is not closed: Red-Diff with a DS prior still wins on LIS and substantially on MRI (Tab. 4), so the 'closing the gap' claim holds only partially.

FMPlug consistently scores lowest on perceptual no-reference metrics (CLIPIQA, e.g., 0.17-0.28 vs. 0.6+ for FlowChef-P in super-resolution), which may indicate bias toward data-fitting/oversmoothed solutions; the appendix dismissal of these metrics (A.4), while defensible, does not fully address whether reconstructions are perceptually competitive.

Some overstatement in framing ('for the first time' identifying the gap; 'paves the way'); the gap itself is arguably a known limitation of generalist priors and the empirical demonstration is confined to Gaussian deblurring, SR, inpainting, and three InverseBench tasks.

Minor presentation issues: broken citation formatting (e.g., 'Patrick Esser et al, 2024'), an empty project-page field, references to Sec. 3.3/A.3 for hyperparameters that are actually in A.3, and typos ('vise versa', 'strenthen'). Reproducibility relies on code not yet linked.

strengths: The paper identifies and clearly documents a real and interesting phenomenon: foundation flow-matching priors underperform domain-specific and even untrained priors when used for inverse problems (Tab. 1, Fig. 3), and this gap is analyzed more carefully than in prior work.

The proposed method is simple and well-motivated at an intuitive level: the learnable warm-start time t (Eq. 3.5) is a sensible generalization of D-Flow's fixed initialization (Eq. 2.4), and the ablation (Tab. 5) and learned-t analysis (Tab. 6) support that the warm-start is the main driver of gains.

The experimental coverage is broad: three image restoration datasets and tasks, three scientific IPs from InverseBench (Tab. 4), ablations on shell thickness and NFE (Tabs. 7-8), robustness to random initialization (Tab. 17), and runtime/memory reporting (Tab. 9).

The few-shot extension (Eq. 3.11) with simplex-constrained instance weights is a reasonable adaptation for scientific imaging, and the correlation analysis between learned weights and instance-to-target distance (Spearman -0.71) is a nice sanity check.
Complete algorithms and detailed hyperparameters are provided in the appendix, and the method's low variance across initializations (Tab. 17) is practically relevant.
weaknesses: Limited technical depth. The two ingredients reduce to (i) making D-Flow's initialization time learnable and (ii) a hard Euclidean projection onto a norm shell (Eq. 3.9), which is a trivial modification of the known spherical constraint (Yang et al., 2024). The 'sharp Gaussianity regularization' contributes marginally: the sensitivity analysis (Tab. 7) shows differences of ~0.1 dB across epsilon values, and the ablation (Tab. 5) attributes most of the gain to the warm-start alone. This is closer to a well-tuned engineering fix than a conceptual advance.

The theoretical motivation is loose and partly unsupported. The claim that G_theta is only valid on a thin shell S and 'wild' on S^c is asserted via a concentration-of-measure argument, but no evidence is provided that off-shell behavior is actually the failure mode of D-Flow. Moreover, the argument is questionable for latent FM models (SD3), whose latent space is not exactly N(0, I); the paper applies the machinery to latent models (Eq. 3.10) without addressing this mismatch.

The central claim of 'closing the gap' to domain-specific priors is only partially supported. In Tab. 16, FMPlug(FD) still trails OT-ODE(DS) and PnP-Flow(DS) on LPIPS/DISTS for both tasks; on scientific IPs (Tab. 4), Red-Diff with a domain-specific prior clearly outperforms FMPlug on MRI (28.71 vs 23.60 PSNR). The paper acknowledges the MRI gap but attributes it to instance placement without a controlled experiment.

The few-shot setting has a circularity problem. The motivation for scientific IPs is precisely that clean ground-truth data is unavailable (Sec. 3.4: 'black holes, nano-materials'), yet the method assumes access to clean instances {x_k} close to the unknown x. For many of the motivating applications, such instances are as hard to obtain as training data, which weakens the practical significance of the scientific-IP contribution.

Potential dismissal of unfavorable evidence. FMPlug consistently underperforms on CLIPIQA (and often MUSIQ) across nearly all tasks, suggesting reconstructions that stay close to the measurement rather than leveraging generative detail. The appendix (A.4) argues these metrics should be de-weighted due to adversarial-robustness concerns; while citations are given, this conveniently excludes the metrics where the method loses, and no user study or perceptual validation is offered.

Baseline and comparison concerns. Domain-specific results are partly quoted from prior papers rather than rerun under identical settings (Tab. 4); recent related plug-in methods (e.g., DMPlug, cited but not compared) are missing; and the NFE framing (NFE=3 vs 28) is misleading given that FMPlug is in fact the slowest method in wall-clock time (492s vs 7-10s in Tab. 9).

Carelessness that undermines confidence: the 'Project page:' placeholder is empty, a reference contains the literal placeholder 'Accessed: [Current Date, e.g., July 28, 2025]', and several citations are formatted inconsistently (e.g., 'Patrick Esser et al', 'Agarwal, Niket et al'), with future-dated references (2026). Together with a small evaluation set (100 images per dataset), this raises reproducibility and polish concerns.

Overstated claims of novelty ('for the first time' identifying the gap; 'first step to address the gap') despite Section 2.3.2 acknowledging that prior works (Ben-Hamu et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2025) already proposed prior-strengthening mechanisms; FMPlug is best viewed as an incremental refinement of these.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly articulated problem: the paper convincingly demonstrates (Tab. 1, Fig. 3, Tab. 16) that foundation FM priors underperform domain-specific and even untrained priors for inverse problems, a real and timely gap that prior work had not explicitly characterized.

The method components are grounded in a coherent high-dimensional argument: the concentration-of-measure (Thm. 3.1) rationale for why D-Flow's initialization (Eq. 2.4) lands outside the training shell, and why the χ² negative log-likelihood regularizer is too flat (Fig. 4), gives the warm-start and shell-constraint designs a principled, if heuristic, justification.

Extensive and careful evaluation: 4 linear tasks × 3 datasets, 3 scientific IPs from InverseBench (including a nonlinear one, BKH), ablations of both ingredients (Tab. 5), sensitivity to shell thickness and NFE (Tabs. 7–8), runtime/memory (Tab. 9), variance across 10 random initializations (Tab. 17), and few-shot count ablation (Tab. 18). This level of experimental diligence is above the norm.

Honest treatment of limitations: the authors openly report where FMPlug loses (CLIPIQA/MUSIQ, the MRI few-shot mismatch in Sec. 4.2), explain why (under-representative guidance instances, supported by the learned-weight correlation analysis), and justify treating no-reference metrics cautiously with citations. The footnote on excluded InverseBench tasks is also transparent.

Good reproducibility support: full algorithms (Algs. 1–2), hyperparameters for all baselines (Sec. A.3), forward-model details for the scientific IPs (Sec. A.6), and the surjectivity sanity-check protocol (Sec. A.2).
weaknesses: Limited technical depth/novelty: both ingredients are simple — a learnable starting time t on the flow path and a norm-shell constraint with closed-form projection. The 'sharp regularization' is essentially the known spherical Gaussian constraint of Yang et al. (2024) with slack, and warm-start is a straightforward time-shift trick; the contribution is primarily empirical.

The theoretical narrative is heuristic and only motivates, not guarantees: claims that Gθ's behavior outside the shell 'can be wild' and that the shifted shell has 'negligible intersection' with the training shell are asserted without formal analysis; the approximation zt ≈ αt y + βt z (Eq. 3.4) with error αt ε is loose since ε is unknown and 'controlled' only by making t learnable — the learned t could settle at a value where the approximation is poor (Tab. 6 shows t* ≈ 0.72–0.83, i.e., the error term αt ε is far from negligible).

The headline 'for the first time' framing of the performance gap is somewhat overstated; related observations exist in the diffusion-prior literature and the paper's own evidence is from a small set of tasks.

Noticeable weaknesses in the results themselves: FMPlug consistently scores lowest or near-lowest on CLIPIQA and often trails on MUSIQ (Tabs. 10–15), and the appendix dismissal of these metrics as unreliable, while cited, risks cherry-picking the metric suite that favors the method; the gain over D-Flow, though consistent, comes at the highest wall-clock time in Tab. 9 (492s vs. 7–10s for interleaving methods).

Scope caveats under-discussed in the main text: the method requires either x ≈ y (simple distortion) or access to instance(s) close to x (few-shot); the MRI case shows sizable degradation when guidance does not cover the test distribution (23.60 vs. 28.71 PSNR for Red-Diff), so the 'approaching domain-specific priors' claim holds only for LIS/BKH and under favorable guidance conditions.

Minor presentation issues: 'Project page:' on p.1 appears empty; several typos and notation slips (e.g., '∥z0∥2 should concentrate sharply around d' should read √d; 'STRENGTH' for 'STRENGTHEN' in Sec. 2.3.2 heading); the claim that prior-strengthening techniques are 'almost useless' rests on a single quick experiment (Tab. 1, FD-S rows).
